2 1 Abstract: The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (ECR-CO2) to produce low 2 carbon fuels and high-value industrial chemicals has been proven to be a viable solution to 3 energy sustainability. However, the energy efficiency of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction is 4 seriously limited by both the poor electrocatalyst with insufficient activity, selectivity and 5 stability, and ineffective electrochemical reactors. In this work, the electroreduction of CO2 6 to CO is highly improved by the design of copper metal organic frameworks-derived 7 nanoparticle (Cu-MOF/NP) catalysts, in which Cu/Cu2O particles form a porous octahedral 8 structure containing tunable Cu0 and Cu+ catalytic active sites. The ECR-CO2 can be 9 realized with a high current density of 25.15 mA cm-2 at a very low applied potential of 10 merely 0.79VRHE even in H-type cell, owing to the high-surface-area porous structure with 11 optimal surface chemistry of exposed Cu cations. Notably, a new flow electrochemical 12 reactor integrating with a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) is designed to not only 13 largely reduce the applied potential ( 200mV), but also prompt the sensitivity of the reactor 14 for identifying and quantifying reaction products. Accordingly, the Cu-MOF/NP catalyst 15 enables an ultrahigh current density beyond 230 mA cm-2 at a low applied potential of - 16 0.86VRHE in the flow MEA reactor, and the ethanol product (often undetectable in the 17 traditional H-type cell) can be harvested.

3 1 INTRODUCTION 2 3 The greenhouse effect and energy crisis are getting worse with the burning of fossil fuels. 4 In order to protect our earth, controlling the content of CO2 in the atmosphere has become 5 the spotlight. Developing new clean energy to replace the original fossil energy is 6 undoubtedly the key to solving the problem, and how to convert CO2 into valuable clean 7 energy is not only the focus of today's scientific research but also the necessary 8 requirements for improving the environment1-3. There are several ways to meet this 9 challenge, including chemical conversion of CO2, photocatalytic reduction of CO2, 10 photoelectrocatalysis reduction of CO2 and electrochemical reduction of CO2 (ECR-CO2) 11 4-5. Among them, the ECR-CO2 is one of the most promising strategies owing to its higher 12 energy efficiency and milder reaction conditions6. However, CO2 is one of a 13 thermodynamically stable molecule that requires a large amounts of energy to activate it to 14 form the CO2 radical anion (ERHE = -1.90 V)7, which is a core involved in the whole 15 reaction processes. Moreover, the energy required for the hydrogen evolution reaction 16 (ERHE = 0 V) is much less than the energy required to activate CO2, resulting in low 17 selectivity to the desired product7. While there is considerable effort made in the quest for 18 new electrocatalysts, there are still numerous challenges to create efficient and economical 19 CO2 reduction catalysts including improving their often low energy efficiency and 20 selectivity, reducing cost, and increasing catalyst durability. 21 Typically, the ECR-CO2 is proceeded through multiple electron reduction reactions 22 in mildly acidic solutions (referred to as the reactions R1 R5)6. Firstly, CO2 - is produced 23 by an one electron transfer, and then various kinds of reduction products are formed

The main products of ECR-CO2 are small 2 organic molecules such as ethylene (C2H4), methanol (CH3OH), ethanol (C2H6O) and 3 inorganic carbon monoxide (CO)6. 4 In order to produce these high value-added chemicals, the most critical step is to 5 convert CO2 to CO10-14. In addition, the as-produced CO can be used with H2 as synthesis 6 gas for Fischer-Tropsch reactions and methanol synthesis15-17. Therefore, many efforts 7 have been devoted to the development of electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion to CO 8 through the engineering of their chemical composition18-20, morphology21, and structures229 23. However, despite of the progress in catalysts exploring, the energy efficiency of the 10 CO2 conversion to CO is still much low because large overpotentials (e.g., -1.0 mA 11 cmL at -0.6 VRHE)20 are often required during the reduction reaction, which cannot meet 12 the needs for practical applications. 13 Compared to the acidic electrolyte system, recent studies seeking on ECR-CO2 14 catalysts have been targeted to the alkaline aqueous electrolyte system due to higher 15 solubility of CO2 and suppression of hydrogen evolution24-25. It is worth to mention that Cu is the only metal catalyst that can further reduce 4 CO to C2, C3 and multiple carbons32-33. Nevertheless, both the activity and selectivity of 5 the Cu catalyst needs to be further improved18-20. 6 Metal organic frameworks (MOF) and their derivatives with open porous structures 7 have been demonstrated to increase the metal active sites for improved electrocatalytic 8 performance. Zheng et al34 reported the MOF-derived nitrogen-doped nanoporous carbon 9 (NC) as a highly efficient catalyst for the conversion of CO2 to CO. The NC catalyst with 10 the best performance achieves high selectivity with 95.4% CO faradaic efficiency (FE) at 11 L+.9 VRHE. Kim et al35 have recently developed MOF-derived Cu nanoparticles (NPs) 12 catalyst by electrochemical reduction of Cu-based MOF-74, which endows high faradaic 13 efficiency (>50%) for the CH4 production. In addition, Albo et al36 synthesized the 14 HKUST-1 MOF catalyst by temperature-assisted solvent-free route, which shows unique 15 advantages in the ECR-CO2 for producing methanol and ethanol. Despite of work applying 16 the MOF-templated method to prepare ECR-CO2 catalyst, the use of this approach to 17 improve the catalytic activity for CO2 electroreduction to CO has rarely been concerned in 18 the literature. 19 In addition to the catalyst development, the design and the engineering of the 20 electrochemical reactor are crucial in the ECR-CO2 performance improvement. In this 21 regard, Lee et al37 reported a H-type cell consisting of a cathode chamber and an anode 22 chamber that are separated by an ion-exchange membrane. However, limitations of this traditional H-type cell, such as the large 2 electrode distance, low accumulation of liquid products, and large pH gradient near 3 electrode surfaces need to be spontaneously addressed for realizing the electrochemical 4 CO2 reduction technology. 5 Other types of ECR-CO2 reactors such as the membrane electrode assembly (MEA)6 integrated stationary reactor39, where CO2 gas flows directly to the catalyst (instead of 7 purging into the electrolyte) and is reduced to form CO, water and H2, have been reported 8 to shorten the electrode distances, thereby reducing the internal resistance and ohmic 9 polarization. Unfortunately, as the product gas (e.g., CO, H2, O2) generation increases at 10 high currents in both the cathode and anode, a thin gas film is formed on the surface of the 11 electrodes, which hinders the accessibility of the electrolyte to the catalyst and prevents the 12 reduction reaction from further proceeding. Moreover, the identification and quantification 13 of gas products has always been an issue in these electrochemical reactors, since the gas 14 products always enters the gas chromatography along with the reaction gas (i.e., CO2), and 15 the exact content of the gas products is difficult to be detected when the gas production rate 16 is low40-42. Therefore, it is necessary to design more advanced reaction devices to enable 17 wide integration of ECR-CO2 for practical applications. 18 Inspired by the above conceptions, in this work, a Cu-MOF-derived nanoparticle 19 catalysts system and a flow MEA reactor with separation of reaction CO2 gas and gas/liquid 20 products have been innovatively established for the electroreduction of CO2 to CO. Such 21 reactor is designed to not only reduce the electrode distance and therefore the overall ohmic 22 polarization of the system, but also increase the sensitivity of identification and 23 quantification of the gas products by increasing the product yield. sections.heading: 12 Physical characterization of Cu-MOF20/300

13 The schematic of the synthesis procedure of the Cu-MOF-derived nanoparticle (Cu14 MOF/NP) catalysts is illustrated in Figure 1a. Cu-MOF octahedral nanoparticles were 15 firstly synthesized by mixing the Cu(NO3)2 3H2O, 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid (H3BTC) 16 and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) in methonal at room temperature for 5 h. Then Cu-MOF 17 octahedrons were pyrolyzed in N2 gas at 300 oC with a heating rate of 20 oC/min. During 18 this process, Cu-MOF octahedrons were reduced to a heterogeneous hybrid of Cu and 19 Cu2O, and the relative proportions of Cu0/Cu+ of the pyrolyzed samples is tunable by 20 different holding temperatures and heating rates. The Cu-MOF octahedrons treated with 21 different temperatures (referred to as y oC) and heating rates (referred to as xoC/min) during 22 the pyrolysis were thus prepared and denoted as Cu-MOFx/y. The octahedral morphology 23 of the Cu-MOF is confirmed by the scanning electron microscope (SEM) (Figure 1b).
